MUJAHID:v1p348#4/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v1p348#4/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v1p348#4/r1.claim: Mujahid says sakar is wine before its prohibition, while good provision is food.

MUQATIL:16:64-67/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:16:64-67/r4.speaker: author
MUQATIL:16:64-67/r4.claim: Sakar means intoxicating drink made from dates or grapes, while good provision means wholesome, non-intoxicating drink and fruit; Muqatil says the intoxicant permission is abrogated by a verse in al-Ma'ida.

MUQATIL:16:64-67/r5.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:16:64-67/r5.speaker: author
MUQATIL:16:64-67/r5.claim: He glosses “goodly loan” in 2:245 as giving with a willing heart, illustrating the sense of good provision.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r2.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r2.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r2.claim: God made the fruits of date palms and grapes available for intoxicants and wholesome provision.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r3.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r3.speaker: ابن مجاهد
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r3.claim: Ibn Mujāhid's father identifies the intoxicant as wine made before its prohibition and wholesome provision as food.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r4.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās distinguishes prohibited fruit products as intoxicants and permitted products as wholesome provision.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r5.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r5.speaker: قتادة
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r5.claim: Qatāda says the verse preceded wine's prohibition; wholesome provision includes eating, pressing, infusing, and pickling the permitted fruit, while sugar refers to foreign wines.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r6.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r6.speaker: أبو موسى الأشعري
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r6.claim: Abū Mūsā lists regional wines: dates and fresh dates in Medina, grapes in Persia, and date honey in Yemen; Ḥammād adds honey and rice wine from Abyssinia.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r7.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r7.speaker: رسول الله
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r7.claim: The Prophet says wine comes from the date palm and grapevine.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r8.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r8.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p72#2/r8.claim: ʿUmar says fermented drinks derive from five ingredients—dates, raisins, honey, wheat, and barley—and whatever is fermented and aged is wine.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p73/r1.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p73/r1.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p73/r1.claim: The sign in the date and grape products is like the preceding sign in milk.

FARRA:v2p109/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p109/r2.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p109/r2.claim: سكر means wine before its prohibition; رزقا حسنا means raisins, dates, and similar provisions.

MAJAZ:v1p363/r1.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p363/r1.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p363/r1.claim: Sukran means flavor or food, something made for tasting.

MAJAZ:v1p363/r2.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p363/r2.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p363/r2.claim: In another usage, sukr means rest: heat subsides, and a still night is called sākirah.

MAJAZ:v1p363/r3.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p363/r3.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p363/r3.claim: Jundal's verse uses sukr for taste.

MAJAZ:v1p363/r4.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p363/r4.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p363/r4.claim: An anonymous line also calls a quiet night sākirah.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p357#4/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p357#4/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p357#4/r1.claim: Qatada says intoxicant refers to foreign wines, later abrogated in al-Ma'ida; good provision is what people infuse, pickle, and eat.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p357#4/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p357#4/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p357#4/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas explains intoxicant as what is forbidden from the fruit and good provision as what is lawful.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p245#2/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p245#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p245#2/r1.claim: Sukr means wine, a reading from before wine was prohibited; good provision means dates and raisins.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p245#2/r2.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p245#2/r2.speaker: أبو عبيدة
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p245#2/r2.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says sukr means food or taste, an interpretation the author says he does not know from tafsīr.

TUSTARI:16:67/r1.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:16:67/r1.speaker: إبراهيم والشعبي
TUSTARI:16:67/r1.claim: Ibrahim and al-Shaʿbi say this verse was abrogated by the verse prohibiting wine.

TUSTARI:16:67/r2.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:16:67/r2.speaker: author
TUSTARI:16:67/r2.claim: For Sahl, intoxication is whatever intoxicates the soul in this world while leaving its consequence in the afterlife uncertain.

TUSTARI:16:67/r3.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:16:67/r3.speaker: أبو حمزة
TUSTARI:16:67/r3.claim: Abu Hamza lists four intoxications: drink, youth, wealth, and political power.

TUSTARI:16:67/r4.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:16:67/r4.speaker: author
TUSTARI:16:67/r4.claim: Sahl adds two forms of intoxication: a scholar’s love of worldly life and a worshipper’s desire to be noticed.

TAB-FULL:v14p274/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p274/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v14p274/r1.claim: The verse omits a noun after “from the fruits,” meaning “some of what comes from the palms and grapes”; من already signals a partitive selection.

TAB-FULL:v14p274/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p274/r2.speaker: بعض نحويي البصرة
TAB-FULL:v14p274/r2.claim: A Basran grammarian supplies شيء as the omitted noun; the pronoun in منه refers to that implied thing, and تتخذون describes it.

TAB-FULL:v14p274/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p274/r3.speaker: بعضهم
TAB-FULL:v14p274/r3.claim: Some interpreters say sakar means wine and good provision means dates and raisins, and that the verse preceded the later prohibition of wine.

TAB-FULL:v14p274/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p274/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v14p274/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets sakar as the prohibited drink and good provision as what is permitted from the fruit.

TAB-FULL:v14p277/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p277/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v14p277/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas repeatedly glosses sakar as what is forbidden from the two fruits and good provision as what is permitted.

TAB-FULL:v14p277/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p277/r2.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
TAB-FULL:v14p277/r2.claim: Sa‘id ibn Jubayr says the forbidden part of the fruits is sakar and the permitted part is good provision.

TAB-FULL:v14p279/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p279/r1.speaker: أبو رزين
TAB-FULL:v14p279/r1.claim: Abu Razin says the verse came while people still drank wine, before its prohibition.

TAB-FULL:v14p279/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p279/r2.speaker: إبراهيم، الشعبي، أبو رزين
TAB-FULL:v14p279/r2.claim: Ibrahim, al-Sha‘bi, and Abu Razin regard the verse as abrogated; Ibrahim specifies that the wine prohibition abrogated it.

TAB-FULL:v14p279/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p279/r3.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v14p279/r3.claim: Al-Hasan says God mentioned wine as a blessing before wine was prohibited; another report contrasts forbidden sakar with permitted provision.

TAB-FULL:v14p281/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p281/r1.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v14p281/r1.claim: Mujahid identifies sakar as wine before its prohibition and good provision as food, or as fresh dates and grapes.

TAB-FULL:v14p281/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p281/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v14p281/r2.claim: Qatada says sakar is foreign wine and good provision includes fermented drinks, vinegar, and food; the verse preceded wine’s later prohibition in al-Ma’ida.

TAB-FULL:v14p281/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p281/r3.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v14p281/r3.claim: Another Qatada report says sakar is foreign wine, later abrogated in al-Ma’ida, while good provision includes fermented drinks, vinegar, and food.

TAB-FULL:v14p281/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p281/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v14p281/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says people called wine sakar; he recounts the Wadi al-Sukran custom of accompanying travelers from Syria and says Abyssinians use sakar for vinegar.

TAB-FULL:v14p281/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p281/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v14p281/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas says good provision means lawful dates, raisins, and other non-intoxicating products.

TAB-FULL:v14p281/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p281/r6.speaker: آخرون
TAB-FULL:v14p281/r6.claim: Another group says sakar is not wine itself but a fermented date or raisin infusion that becomes intoxicating and is prohibited like wine.

TAB-FULL:v14p283/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p283/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v14p283/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says the verse preceded wine’s prohibition and that intoxicating sakar is forbidden like wine; lawful provision includes dates, raisins, and vinegar.

TAB-FULL:v14p283/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p283/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v14p283/r2.claim: He says that after wine was prohibited, sakar was also prohibited as part of wine, while vinegar, lawful nabidh, and similar drinks remained permitted.

TAB-FULL:v14p283/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p283/r3.speaker: عبد الله
TAB-FULL:v14p283/r3.claim: Abdullah, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibrahim, and Ibrahim with Abu Razin identify sakar as wine.

TAB-FULL:v14p283/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p283/r4.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v14p283/r4.claim: Al-Dahhak defines sakar as whatever intoxicates from grapes or dates, and good provision as their fruit.

TAB-FULL:v14p283/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p283/r5.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v14p283/r5.claim: Ibn Zayd says the fruit was lawful until people altered it and made sakar from it.

TAB-FULL:v14p283/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p283/r6.speaker: آخرون
TAB-FULL:v14p283/r6.claim: Another group takes sakar to mean any lawful drink such as non-intoxicating nabidh, vinegar, or fresh dates, and good provision as dates and raisins.

TAB-FULL:v14p284/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p284/r1.speaker: الشعبي
TAB-FULL:v14p284/r1.claim: Al-Sha‘bi rejects the Nabataean intoxicating drink as sakar here; the verse means lawful nabidh or vinegar, with dates and raisins as good provision.

TAB-FULL:v14p284/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p284/r2.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v14p284/r2.claim: Mujahid says people made nabidh from dates and used dates and raisins as food or good provision.

TAB-FULL:v14p284/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p284/r3.speaker: الشعبي
TAB-FULL:v14p284/r3.claim: Al-Sha‘bi again identifies sakar with nabidh and vinegar, and provision with dates and raisins.

TAB-FULL:v14p284/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p284/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v14p284/r4.claim: Al-Tabari prefers the lawful-drink interpretation, under which the verse remains in force rather than abrogated.

TAB-FULL:v14p284/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p284/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v14p284/r5.claim: Sakar has four Arabic senses: intoxicating drink, food, stillness, and the verbal noun for becoming intoxicated; poetry illustrates food and stillness.

TAB-FULL:v14p284/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p284/r6.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v14p284/r6.claim: Because intoxicants are prohibited but the verse supplies no proof that non-intoxicating lawful fruit drinks are forbidden or abrogated, al-Tabari rules out wine, intoxicants, sakar itself, and stillness here.

TAB-FULL:v14p286/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p286/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v14p286/r1.claim: The blessings of livestock, palms, and grapevines are clear signs for people who understand God’s proofs and heed His admonitions.

ZAJJAJ:v3p209/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p209/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p209/r1.claim: The fruits of palms and grapes are a sign of God's oneness; سكر is interpreted as wine from before its prohibition, and good provision as edible grapes and dates.

ZAJJAJ:v3p209/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p209/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p209/r2.claim: Another interpretation takes سكر as food and cites an unattributed line using سكرا; the author says the wine interpretation fits better.

NAHHAS:v2p402/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p402/r1.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p402/r1.claim: The date palms and grapes God provided contain a lesson for people.

THALABI:v6p26/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p26/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v6p26/r10.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas says sakar is what is prohibited from the fruits, and good provision is what is lawful.

THALABI:v6p26/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p26/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p26/r7.claim: Fruit from palms and grapes is another sign; منه refers back to those fruits.

THALABI:v6p26/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p26/r8.speaker: قوم
THALABI:v6p26/r8.claim: One group says sakar is wine, while good provision means vinegar, grapes, dates, and raisins; this is associated with the view that wine is forbidden.

THALABI:v6p26/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p26/r9.speaker: ابن مسعود
THALABI:v6p26/r9.claim: Ibn Masud, Ibn Amr, and several others are named with the view that sakar means the forbidden product of the fruit and good provision its lawful products.

THALABI:v6p27/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p27/r1.speaker: مقاتل
THALABI:v6p27/r1.claim: The continuation says sakar includes foreign peoples' wine, while good provision is what people ferment, make into vinegar, or eat.

THALABI:v6p27/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p27/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p27/r2.claim: The verse came before wine was prohibited; its prohibition came later in Surat al-Maida.

THALABI:v6p27/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p27/r3.speaker: الشعبي
THALABI:v6p27/r3.claim: Al-Shabi says sakar is what one drinks and good provision what one eats.

THALABI:v6p27/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p27/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v6p27/r4.claim: Al-Awfi transmits Ibn Abbas's statement that Ethiopians use sakar for vinegar.

THALABI:v6p27/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p27/r5.speaker: الضحاك
THALABI:v6p27/r5.claim: Another view defines sakar as intoxicating date or raisin infusion once strong, or cooked juice; authorities include al-Dahhak, al-Shabi, al-Nakha'i, and Ibn Abbas in a report.

THALABI:v6p27/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p27/r6.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p27/r6.claim: A Prophetic report distinguishes wine from grapes, sakar from dates, bit from honey, mazr from corn, and bayra from wheat, then forbids every intoxicant.

THALABI:v6p27/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p27/r7.speaker: أبو عبيدة
THALABI:v6p27/r7.claim: Abu Ubayda glosses sakar as taste or flavor, as in saying that something is a flavor for you.

THALABI:v6p27/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p27/r8.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p27/r8.claim: An unnamed poet uses sakar to mean flavor.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r10.speaker: الشعبي والسدي
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r10.claim: Another interpretation takes السكر as intoxicating nabidh and good provision as dates and raisins; Iraqi jurists cited the verse as evidence that nabidh is permitted.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r11.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r11.claim: A third interpretation gives السكر the Abyssinian meaning vinegar and takes good provision to mean food.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r12.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r12.speaker: أبو جعفر الطبري
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r12.claim: Al-Tabari takes sugar as food tasted and lawful to drink from palm and grape fruits, thus identifying it with good provision.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r6.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة وسعيد بن جبير
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r6.claim: سكر means wine, while good provision means dates, fresh dates, and raisins; the verse preceded the prohibition of wine. Ibn Abbas distinguishes forbidden drink from lawful fruit.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r7.speaker: قتادة
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r7.claim: On the wine interpretation, the verse may have permitted wine and then been abrogated by the prohibition.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r8.claim: Alternatively, the verse reports that people made wine even though it was not lawful for them.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r9.speaker: الأخطل
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p197/r9.claim: Al-Akhtal's poem uses السكر for wine and المزاء for an intoxicating nabidh.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p198/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p198/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p198/r1.claim: A poetic citation, وجعلت عيب الأكرمين سكرا, is evidence for the interpretation of sugar as food or something tasted and lawful.

QUSHAYRI:v2p161/r13.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p161/r13.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p161/r13.claim: God also grants people many forms of benefit from date palms, including fresh and dried dates.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p116/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p116/r1.speaker: صاحب النظم
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p116/r1.claim: He supplies an omitted relative phrase: from the fruits of palms and grapes you take from them an intoxicant; otherwise the pronoun would need to be feminine plural.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p116/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p116/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p116/r2.claim: Arabic may omit ma and min, as in the cited verses.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p116/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p116/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p116/r3.claim: Grapes are coordinated with the fruits, not with palms; otherwise the phrase would oddly mean fruits of grapes rather than fruit and grapes.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p116/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p116/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p116/r4.claim: In reports from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Shahr ibn Hawshab, and ʿAmr ibn Sufyan, intoxicant means what is forbidden from the two fruits and good provision what is permitted; in Ata's report, it means intoxicating drink before wine was prohibited.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p117/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p117/r1.speaker: عامة المفسرين
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p117/r1.claim: Most commentators identify sakar as wine and good provision as lawful products such as vinegar, raisins, and dates; they say the verse preceded wine's prohibition in al-Maʾida.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p117/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p117/r2.speaker: الفراء والزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p117/r2.claim: They choose the lexical meaning wine for sakar; Jarir's line uses sakar in that sense.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p117/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p117/r3.speaker: أبو عبيدة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p117/r3.claim: He alone says sakar means food, citing poetry where a speaker makes the nobles' reputations his food.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p117/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p117/r4.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p117/r4.claim: He rejects the food interpretation as less fitting than wine and reads the poem as saying the speaker intoxicates himself with the nobles' reputations.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p120/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p120/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p120/r1.claim: Those who reason recognize God unique power, affirm His prophet, and become certain of reward and punishment.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:16:66-68/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:16:66-68/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:16:66-68/r2.claim: The intoxicant made from dates and grapes is wine; this verse preceded wine's prohibition, while good provision means vinegar, raisins, and dates.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:16:66-68/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:16:66-68/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:16:66-68/r3.claim: These fruits are a sign for people who understand God's power.

JISHUMI:v6p4066#2/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4066#2/r1.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v6p4066#2/r1.claim: Sukr has four lexical senses: an intoxicating drink; food or flavor; stillness or quiet; and the verbal noun for becoming confused or blocked, including blocked water channels.

JISHUMI:v6p4066#2/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4066#2/r2.speaker: الشاعر
JISHUMI:v6p4066#2/r2.claim: The cited line ‘they made the best people's grapes sukr’ uses sukr to mean food or flavor.

JISHUMI:v6p4066#2/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4066#2/r3.speaker: الشاعر
JISHUMI:v6p4066#2/r3.claim: The cited phrases use sukr for stillness, including a calm night, a wind that has settled, and the eye of a slaughtered camel.

JISHUMI:v6p4066#2/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4066#2/r5.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v6p4066#2/r5.claim: The pronoun in منه refers to an omitted ‘thing’: from the fruits people take an intoxicant; رزقا حسنا may be coordinated with it, as Abū Muslim says, or supplied by a separate verb.

JISHUMI:v6p4071/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4071/r3.speaker: مشايخنا
JISHUMI:v6p4071/r3.claim: They infer that a cooked drink is permissible: since the verse counts sukr as a blessing but wine is forbidden, sukr here must be cooked drink; an abrogation claim is unnecessary when reconciliation works.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r1.claim: The pronoun in minhu points to an omitted mā: what people make from date-palm and grape fruits.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r2.claim: A group takes sakar as wine and good provision as vinegar, raisins, dates, and date syrup; they say this preceded wine's prohibition.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r3.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عمر وسعيد بن جبير والحسن ومجاهد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r3.claim: They hold the interpretation that sakar means wine and that the verse preceded its prohibition.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r4.speaker: الشعبي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r4.claim: He interprets sakar as what people drink and good provision as what they eat.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r5.claim: The report through al-ʿAwfī says sakar means vinegar in Abyssinian usage.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r6.speaker: الضحاك والنخعي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r6.claim: They take sakar to mean intoxicating nabīdh, including fermented date or raisin infusion and cooked juice.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r7.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r7.claim: Those who permit or forbid nabīdh agree that the verse reports what people make; it does not itself make it lawful.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r8.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p28#2/r8.claim: The strongest view is that the sakar clause was abrogated; Ibn Abbas distinguishes forbidden fruit products from lawful provision.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r1.claim: The fruit phrase may depend on an omitted we give you drink, be governed by you make, repeat a preposition for emphasis, or describe an omitted noun meaning fruit from which you make drink and provision.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r2.claim: If minhu is a repeated prepositional phrase, its pronoun refers to the omitted juice, as a pronoun may refer to an omitted noun elsewhere.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r3.claim: Sukr means wine and is derived from the verbal noun for becoming intoxicated; the author cites a poem using the word.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r4.speaker: الشعبي
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r4.claim: Al-Shaʿbī and al-Nakhaʿī are among those who hold that this verse was abrogated.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r5.claim: An alternative is to combine the verse's reproach with its expression of divine favor.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r6.speaker: أبو حنيفة
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r6.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa's view takes sukr as fermented nabīdh made from grape, raisin, or date juice, permissible until it intoxicates; he adduces this verse and a report.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r7.speaker: أبو علي الجبائي
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r7.claim: Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī wrote books permitting nabīdh but declined to drink it in old age, saying consumption seemed indecent and unbecoming of good character.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r8.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r8.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r8.claim: Other readings take sukr to mean taste, or something like wine through indulging in people's reputations; good provision includes vinegar, syrup, dates, raisins, and similar foods.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r9.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r9.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p575#2/r9.claim: Sukr itself may be construed as good provision, with the phrase meaning that people make from fruit both intoxicant and wholesome provision.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r1.speaker: الطبري
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r1.claim: Al-Tabari supplies an omitted relative clause: from the fruits are things that you take.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r10.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r10.claim: A sound prophetic report says wine itself is prohibited and so is anything else intoxicating; Iraqis transmitted a different vocalization associated with their rule allowing small amounts of other drinks.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r2.speaker: فرقة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r2.claim: Another group supplies an omitted word meaning some or a thing that you take from the fruits.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r3.claim: The phrase may coordinate with livestock as another sign and blessing, or with the previous مِن phrase as another drink made from fruit.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says this verse preceded the prohibition of wine: السكر means wine and good provision means lawful food and drink from dates and grapes.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r5.speaker: ابن جبير وإبراهيم والشعبي وأبو زيد
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r5.claim: Ibn Jubayr, Ibrahim, al-Shaʿbi, and Abu Zayd share the reading that السكر is wine before the prohibition and good provision is other lawful food and drink.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r6.speaker: الحسن بن أبي الحسن
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r6.claim: Al-Hasan says God mentioned the blessing of intoxicating drink before wine was prohibited.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r7.speaker: الشعبي ومجاهد
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r7.claim: Al-Shaʿbi and Mujahid take sugar to mean a wholesome, non-intoxicating drink such as vinegar, syrup, or nabīdh; good provision means dates and grapes.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r8.speaker: الطبري
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r8.claim: Al-Tabari says sugar can mean food in Arabic and prefers that reading, which includes no wine and requires no abrogation.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r9.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p405#2/r9.claim: Some who identify sugar as wine say the verse was abrogated by the wine prohibition, but the author calls this flawed because abrogation concerns an established legal ruling.

TABRISI:16:66-67/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-67/r10.speaker: قتادة
TABRISI:16:66-67/r10.claim: Qatāda says the verse was revealed before wine was prohibited and that its prohibition came later in Sūrat al-Māʾida.

TABRISI:16:66-67/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-67/r11.speaker: أبو مسلم
TABRISI:16:66-67/r11.claim: Abū Muslim says there is no need to place the verse before the prohibition: it addresses polytheists and counts their blessings, including wine as one of their drinks.

TABRISI:16:66-67/r12.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-67/r12.speaker: الشعبي
TABRISI:16:66-67/r12.claim: Al-Shaʿbī and al-Jubbāʾī interpret ‘intoxicant’ as permissible kinds of drink and ‘good provision’ as food, the pleasant things people eat.

TABRISI:16:66-67/r13.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-67/r13.speaker: الجبائي
TABRISI:16:66-67/r13.claim: Al-Shaʿbī and al-Jubbāʾī interpret ‘intoxicant’ as permissible kinds of drink and ‘good provision’ as food, the pleasant things people eat.

TABRISI:16:66-67/r14.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-67/r14.speaker: author
TABRISI:16:66-67/r14.claim: The verse does not authorize nabīdh: it reports what people did with the fruits, just as another verse reports making oaths a means of deception; describing a use does not license it.

TABRISI:16:66-67/r15.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-67/r15.speaker: author
TABRISI:16:66-67/r15.claim: God created these fruits for people’s benefit, but people also made forbidden things from them.

TABRISI:16:66-67/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-67/r5.speaker: الحسن
TABRISI:16:66-67/r5.claim: One construction means that people have a lesson in what God produced from the fruits of palms and grapes.

TABRISI:16:66-67/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-67/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:16:66-67/r6.claim: Another construction supplies the omitted relative ‘what’: from the fruits of palms and grapes, you make what becomes an intoxicant; Arabs often omit the relative pronoun.

TABRISI:16:66-67/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-67/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:16:66-67/r7.claim: A further construction supplies an omitted noun: ‘something’ from the fruits of palms and grapes that you make into an intoxicant.

TABRISI:16:66-67/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-67/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:16:66-67/r8.claim: The intoxicant is wine or any intoxicating drink, while good provision is lawful products such as vinegar, raisins, syrup, fresh dates, and dried dates, according to several early authorities.

TABRISI:16:66-67/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-67/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:16:66-67/r9.claim: In a report preserved by al-Ḥākim, Ibn ʿAbbās says ‘intoxicant’ is what is forbidden from the fruits and ‘good provision’ what is lawful.

TABRISI:16:66-70#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-70#2/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:16:66-70#2/r2.claim: In ‘from it you make an intoxicant,’ the pronoun can refer to the fruits already mentioned or to thamarāt as a collective equivalent to thamar.

TABRISI:16:66-70/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-70/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:16:66-70/r7.claim: Sukr has four senses: an intoxicating drink; food or taste, as in the poet’s line about making nobles’ faults a taste; stillness, as in a quiet night or wind; and the verbal noun of sakira, including confusion of sight.

TABRISI:16:66-70/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-70/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:16:66-70/r8.claim: Dhulul is the plural of dhalul, while radhil and radhāl mean low or poor quality.

TABRISI:16:67-69/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:67-69/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:16:67-69/r1.claim: The variety of useful fruit products is a sign for people who reason; God’s extraction of juice from mixed fruit points to His ability to recover the dispersed dead from soil.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r1.claim: The construction omits “something”: from date palms and grapes you take a thing for drink and good provision; minhu refers to the omitted noun.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r2.speaker: الأخفش
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r2.claim: Al-Akhfash says the pronoun is singular because an understood “thing” is omitted; it therefore need not be dual.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r3.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عمر والحسن وسعيد بن جبير ومجاهد والزجاج وابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r3.claim: These authorities interpret sukar as wine; Ibn Abbas reports it means the prohibited drink made from the fruit.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r4.speaker: سعيد بن جبير ومجاهد والشعبي والنخعي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r4.claim: They say this verse initially allowed wine, then was abrogated by the command to avoid it.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r5.speaker: العوفي عن ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r5.claim: Al-Awfi transmits from Ibn Abbas that sukar means vinegar in Abyssinian usage.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r6.speaker: الضحاك
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r6.claim: Al-Dahhak says sukar means vinegar in the language of Yemen.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r7.speaker: أبو عبيدة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r7.claim: Abu Ubayda interprets sukar as taste or flavor, supporting the usage with poetry.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r8.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r8.claim: If sukar means vinegar or flavor, the verse remains operative rather than abrogated.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r9.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p464/r9.claim: Good provision means lawful products such as dates, grapes, raisins, and vinegar.

RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r1.claim: To explain wine's mention as a blessing, one answer says the sura is Meccan and wine was not forbidden until the Ma'ida revelation.

RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r2.claim: Another answer needs no abrogation: wine was useful to the polytheist audience, but separating السكر from good provision signals that it is not good in religious law and is therefore forbidden.

RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r3.speaker: أبو حنيفة
RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r3.claim: A second interpretation takes sugar as nabīdh: grape, raisin, or date juice boiled until two-thirds evaporates and left to ferment; Abu Hanifa permits it until it intoxicates.

RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r4.speaker: أبو حنيفة
RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r4.claim: This view argues that the verse presents sugar as a blessing and that the report wine is forbidden in itself means sugar is something other than wine, namely cooked nabīdh.

RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r5.speaker: أبو عبيدة
RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r5.claim: A third interpretation takes السكر as food; Abu Ubayda supports it with a poetic line where slandering the honorable is made one's food.

RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r6.speaker: الزجاج
RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r6.claim: Al-Zajjaj says the poetic usage better resembles wine: the speaker is metaphorically intoxicated by slandering honorable people.

RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p55#2/r7.claim: The production of these benefits is evidence and blessing; a rational person recognizes that only God can bring about these states and infers a powerful, wise deity.

RAZI-FULL:v20p55/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p55/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p55/r3.claim: After animal benefits, the passage turns to benefits from plants.

RAZI-FULL:v20p55/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p55/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p55/r4.claim: The phrase from dates and grapes attaches to an omitted نسقيكم, meaning their juice, which is omitted because the preceding verb supplies it; تتخذون منه سكرًا explains the drink.

RAZI-FULL:v20p55/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p55/r5.speaker: الواحدي
RAZI-FULL:v20p55/r5.claim: Al-Wahidi says الأعناب coordinates with الثمرات, not النخيل, since grapes themselves are fruit and do not produce another fruit.

RAZI-FULL:v20p55/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p55/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p55/r6.claim: One interpretation takes السكر as wine, a verbal noun of sakira; رزق حسن means other date and grape products such as syrup, vinegar, molasses, dates, and raisins.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#2/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#2/r1.claim: Good provision means what God permits from the two fruits; another interpretation makes the clause a rhetorical question condemning the choice of intoxicants over vinegar, raisins, and dates.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#2/r2.speaker: أبو عبيدة
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#2/r2.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says sukr means taste or food, citing a poem where making someone's faults one's sukr means tasting or relishing them.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#2/r3.speaker: الطبري
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#2/r3.claim: Al-Ṭabarī chooses the food-and-drink sense: sukr and good provision name the same lawful fruit produce in different words, so there is no abrogation.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#2/r4.speaker: الزجاج
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#2/r4.claim: Al-Zajjāj says Abū ʿUbayda's sense is unknown and contradicts the commentators; the poem is no proof because it describes becoming intoxicated by others' faults.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#2/r5.speaker: الحنفيون
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#2/r5.claim: The Ḥanafīs take sukr as non-intoxicating nabīdh and infer it is lawful from the verse's language of divine favor; it becomes forbidden once it intoxicates, supported by two reports about wine and diluted drinks.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#2/r6.speaker: ابن عمر
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#2/r6.claim: A report attributed through ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Nāfiʿ says Ibn ʿUmar saw the Prophet dilute a strong drink with water until it was drinkable and advise breaking the vessels' strength with water.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r1.speaker: النبي
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r1.claim: A report says the Prophet drank the prepared nabīdh that day and gave it to a servant after it changed on the second or third day; the author uses this to argue it was not forbidden.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r2.speaker: الطحاوي
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r2.claim: Al-Ṭaḥāwī cites a report from Ibn ʿAbbās that wine itself, little or much, is forbidden, whereas intoxicating drinks other than wine are not forbidden by their essence.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r3.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r3.claim: A report from ʿUmar says nabīdh is what cuts camel meat in the stomach; al-Sawrī was also seen drinking nabīdh at Mālik ibn Maʿwal's home.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r4.claim: The Ḥanafī argument from divine favor is sound in itself but may refer to the period before wine was prohibited, making the verse abrogated as explained earlier.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r5.speaker: ابن العربي
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r5.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī argues that reports containing legal judgments can be abrogated because the report entails a legal demand; only reports of actual facts or divine reward are not abrogated.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r6.claim: Al-Qurṭubī calls Ibn al-ʿArabī's polemic against opponents excessive, but agrees that the correct legal-theory position allows abrogating a report about a ruling, supported by 16:101.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#3/r7.claim: The first two reports used by the Ḥanafīs are weak; stronger prophetic reports state that every intoxicant is forbidden and that what intoxicates in large quantity is forbidden in small quantity, with al-Nasāʾī defending the transmitters' reliability.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r1.claim: The third report is authentic but the Prophet gave the changed-smelling nabīdh to a servant because he disliked its odor, not because it intoxicated; the same concern explains the report about Zaynab's honey and maghāfīr.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r2.speaker: عطاء
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās is also reported by ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs, and Mujāhid to say that what intoxicates in quantity is forbidden in small quantity; this is also related by Qays ibn Dīnār and is his legal opinion.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r3.claim: The report through ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shaddād conflicts with the larger group and established prophetic teaching, so it cannot support the opposing position.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r4.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r4.claim: ʿUmar's nabīdh meant a non-intoxicating drink; al-Nasāʾī reports it had been turned into vinegar, and another report says ʿUmar punished a drinker if the drink proved intoxicating.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r5.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r5.claim: In a sermon, ʿUmar says wine's prohibition covers drinks made from grapes, honey, dates, wheat, and barley, and defines wine by its effect on the intellect.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r6.speaker: إبراهيم النخعي
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r6.claim: Al-Nasāʾī says Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī was the first to permit intoxicating nabīdh; al-Qurṭubī calls this a learned scholar's error and says no opinion overrides the Sunna.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r7.speaker: ابن المبارك
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r7.claim: Ibn al-Mubārak says the only reliably transmitted concession for intoxicants was from Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r8.speaker: الطحاوي
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#4/r8.claim: Even if reports of al-Ṭaḥāwī or al-Thawrī permitting it are sound, they cannot override the Sunna; al-Ṭaḥāwī elsewhere says the community agrees that fermented, foaming grape juice is wine and that permitting it is unbelief, while date-wine is disputed.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#5/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#5/r1.speaker: الطحاوي
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#5/r1.claim: Al-Ṭaḥāwī argues that the report calling wine a product of date palm and grape was not acted upon as applying the prohibition to date wine; nevertheless, the jurists analogize intoxicating date and raisin infusions and thus every intoxicating drink.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#5/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#5/r2.speaker: الطحاوي
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#5/r2.claim: Al-Ṭaḥāwī accepts the report that every intoxicant is forbidden but says scholars differ whether it means the whole category that can intoxicate or only a drink that actually causes drunkenness.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#5/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#5/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#5/r3.claim: Al-Qurṭubī concludes that al-Ṭaḥāwī's own reasoning makes every intoxicating drink prohibited.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#5/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#5/r4.speaker: عائشة
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#5/r4.claim: ʿĀʾisha says wine is forbidden for its consequence rather than its name, so every drink with the same consequence is forbidden.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#5/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#5/r5.speaker: ابن المنذر
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#5/r5.claim: Ibn al-Mundhir says the Kufans brought defective reports; disputes must return to Qur'an and Sunna, and a successor's drinking is either mistaken interpretation or a sin requiring repentance.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#5/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#5/r6.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67#5/r6.claim: An alternative interpretation treats the fruits as evidence for resurrection: their Creator can resurrect, regardless of whether wine is lawful, and mentioning its use does not itself imply prohibition, as in 2:219.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r1.speaker: الطبري
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r1.claim: Al-Ṭabarī supplies an omitted mā after dates and grapes, with minhu signaling the ellipsis; another view supplies a generic thing, while the preferred parse takes minhu as referring to the mentioned produce without deletion.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r2.claim: Alternatively, the fruit phrase may coordinate with cattle to mean there is a lesson in dates and grapes, or with the preceding min to mean drinks are also provided from fruit.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the verse preceded wine's prohibition: sukr means wine, while good provision is lawful food and drink from the two trees; Ibn Jubayr, al-Nakhaʿī, al-Shaʿbī, and Abū Thawr agree.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r4.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r4.claim: One view takes sukr as vinegar in Abyssinian and good provision as food; another takes it as sweet lawful juice that may later ferment and become forbidden when intoxicating.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r5.speaker: ابن العربي
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r5.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī calls Ibn ʿAbbās's view strongest and offers either pre-prohibition timing or a contrast between people's unlawful use and lawful use; he concludes the Meccan verse was abrogated by the Medinan wine ban.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r6.claim: Al-Qurṭubī says no abrogation is needed if sukr means vinegar or sweet juice, leaving the verse decisive and in force.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r7.speaker: ابن مسعود
QURTUBI-FULL:16:67/r7.claim: Most commentators, including Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿUmar, Abū Razīn, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, Ibn Abī Laylā, and al-Kalbī, define sukr as forbidden wine and good provision as what God permits; language authorities likewise use it for wine or intoxicants, with poetry attesting sukr.

BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r1.claim: The first clause has an omitted verb meaning that people are given the juice of dates and grapes; the following clause resumes the explanation, with its pronoun referring to the omitted juice or fruit.

BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r2.claim: The good provision includes dates, raisins, syrup, and vinegar.

BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r3.claim: If revealed before wine's prohibition, the verse indicates disapproval of it; if afterward, it combines reproach with a reminder of blessing.

BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r4.speaker: قيل
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r4.claim: Sugar is interpreted as nabidh, a fermented drink.

BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r5.speaker: قيل
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r5.claim: Sugar is also said to mean taste or flavor, supported by a poetic use describing grazing on people's reputations.

BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r6.speaker: قيل
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r6.claim: Another interpretation is food that removes hunger, with provision then referring to its sale proceeds.

BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r7.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r7.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:67/r7.claim: The sign benefits people who use reason to examine the evidence.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p262/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p262/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p262/r1.claim: The phrase is attached to an omitted 'We give you drink' from date-palm and grape fruits, meaning their juice; the omission is supplied by the preceding verb.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p262/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p262/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p262/r2.claim: The clause about making sugar explains the drinking or repeats minhu for emphasis; the pronoun returns to the omitted juice.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p262/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p262/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p262/r3.claim: Sukr means wine, named by its verbal noun; alternatively, the verse predates wine's prohibition and is abrogated, or it combines a reproach with a blessing.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p262/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p262/r4.speaker: أبو حنيفة وأبو يوسف
NASAFI-FULL:v2p262/r4.claim: They hold that nabīdh from grapes, raisins, or dates boiled until two-thirds evaporate and then fermented remains lawful until it intoxicates; they argue from this verse, a prophetic report, and many reports.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p262/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p262/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p262/r5.claim: The good provision includes vinegar, syrup, dates, raisins, and other wholesome products.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p262/r6.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p262/r6.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p262/r6.claim: The signs in these fruits are evidence for people who reason.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r2.claim: من ثمرات most naturally attaches to تتخذون; repeating من is emphatic and the singular pronoun can stand for an omitted عصير, the fruit collectively, or an understood antecedent.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r3.claim: Other parses connect the phrase to نسقيكم, coordinate it with livestock as a sign, or supply an omitted ما; the author rejects al-Ṭabarī's proposed deletion as unacceptable to Basran grammarians and notes al-Zamakhsharī's omitted noun analysis.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r4.claim: سكر means wine in Arabic, supported by poetry; al-Zamakhsharī derives it as a verbal noun from سكِر.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r5.speaker: ابن مسعود
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r5.claim: Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿUmar, Abū Razīn, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, al-Shaʿbī, al-Nakhaʿī, Ibn Abī Laylā, al-Kalbī, Ibn Jubayr, Abū Thawr, and most exegetes take السكر as wine; the verse is Meccan, before wine's Medinan prohibition, and thus abrogated on this reading.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r6.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r6.claim: Al-Ḥasan says God mentions wine as a blessing before its prohibition.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says السكر means vinegar in the Ethiopian language; another view takes it as sweet, lawful juice named for what it may become if left to ferment.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r8.speaker: أبو عبيدة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p557/r8.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says السكر means taste and al-Ṭabarī chooses this sense, citing usage and a poetic witness continued in the next passage.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r1.claim: The cited verse uses سكرا for something savored; another interpretation treats wine metaphorically as fermented from human faults.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r2.speaker: الزجاج
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r2.claim: Al-Zajjāj rejects Abū ʿUbayda's meaning of taste as inconsistent with Arab usage and most commentators; views such as vinegar, sweet juice, or non-intoxicating drink avoid abrogation.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r3.speaker: أبو حنيفة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r3.claim: Another view defines النبيذ as grape, raisin, or date juice boiled until two-thirds evaporate, then fermented; Abū Ḥanīfa permits it until intoxication.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r4.claim: If السكر is wine, the verse is abrogated; without that reading it is not. If no abrogation is assumed, the verse combines reproach for forbidden drink with favor for lawful vinegar, date, raisin, or syrup.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r5.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r5.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī permits treating السكر as a kind of رزق حسن, a coordination of qualities; the author observes that ordinary coordination suggests distinct items.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r6.claim: The opening and closing of the livestock sign frame the passage: reason is needed to recognize its lesson.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r7.claim: God says We give milk because animals supply it without human processing; for fruit drinks people process produce, so the verse says you make them.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p558/r8.claim: Milk is presented before fruit drinks and honey because people need it more and it is natural nourishment; the Prophet chose milk when offered milk, wine, and honey on the Night Journey, and the sequence matches the rivers of Paradise.

SAMIN-DURR:16:67#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:67#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:67#2/r1.claim: سكر may directly mean wine, as in a poem pairing it with المِزاء.

SAMIN-DURR:16:67#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:67#2/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:16:67#2/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says سكر was originally a verbal noun, then named wine.

SAMIN-DURR:16:67#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:67#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
SAMIN-DURR:16:67#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says سكر is the Abyssinian word for vinegar.

SAMIN-DURR:16:67#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:67#2/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:67#2/r4.claim: Another view names sweet grape juice سكر because it could later ferment.

SAMIN-DURR:16:67#2/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:67#2/r5.speaker: أبو عبيدة
SAMIN-DURR:16:67#2/r5.claim: Abu Ubayd defines سكر as taste or flavor, citing جعلت أعراض الكرام سكرا.

SAMIN-DURR:16:67#2/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:67#2/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:67#2/r6.claim: A competing gloss takes the poem's سكرا as wine, metaphorically consumed by violating others' honor.

SAMIN-DURR:16:67#3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:67#3/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:67#3/r1.claim: رزقا حسنا most naturally coordinates contrasting products, explained as raisins, vinegar, and similar foods.

SAMIN-DURR:16:67#3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:67#3/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:67#3/r2.claim: Alternatively, both words describe one product that combines intoxication and good nourishment.

SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r1.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r1.claim: Al-Zamakhshari supplies an omitted ونسقيكم من the fruits, meaning their juice; تتخذون explains that provision.

SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r10.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r10.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r10.claim: Al-Zamakhshari supplies ثمر and cites poetry omitting رجل after بكفي, though that deletion is rare without من.

SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r2.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r2.claim: Abu al-Baqa supplies خلق لكم وجعل لكم instead.

SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r3.claim: The author prefers the omitted نسقيكم: the expressed verb explains the livestock lesson and does not naturally govern the fruit phrase.

SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r4.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r4.claim: The Shaikh allows coordination with the prior نسقيكم or an omitted repetition; the author retains his semantic objection.

SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r5.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r5.claim: A second parse attaches ومن ثمرات to تتخذون, with منه repeating the phrase for emphasis.

SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r6.claim: Under that parse, منه can refer to omitted juice, fruits, palms, a genus, a subset, or the stated object.

SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r7.claim: A third parse coordinates it with في الأنعام, making both part of إن's predicate and تتخذون explanatory of the lesson.

SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r8.speaker: الطبري
SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r8.claim: A fourth parse makes the phrase predicate of an omitted subject, estimated by al-Tabari as ما تتخذون; the Shaikh says Basrans disallow it.

SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r9.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:67/r9.claim: The author replies that ما may be an indefinite noun with a clausal adjective; deletion after من is regular, as in 37:164.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p580#3/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p580#3/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p580#3/r1.claim: Camels, cattle, and sheep are signs of the Creator's power, wisdom, gentleness, and mercy.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p581#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p581#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p581#2/r1.claim: Mentioning reason alongside this sign is apt because reason is humanity's noblest faculty; God prohibited intoxicating drinks to preserve it.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p581#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p581#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p581#2/r2.claim: The passage also connects date and grape gardens and their produce to signs of God's creative power, as in 36:34–36.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p581/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p581/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p581/r1.claim: The verse recalls intoxicating date and grape drinks people made before prohibition and thus indicates their earlier legal permissibility; it equates drinks from grapes and dates, as Malik, al-Shafii, Ahmad, and most scholars hold, and the same rule applies to drinks made from grain and honey according to the Sunnah.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p581/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p581/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p581/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets 'intoxicant and good provision' as the forbidden and lawful products of the two fruits; a second narration states the same contrast.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p581/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p581/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p581/r3.claim: Lawful products include dried dates and raisins, syrup, vinegar, and nabidh consumed before it becomes strong, as the Sunnah reports.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r10.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r10.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r10.claim: The verse uses iḥtibāk: mentioning “sukr” implies its opposite in the second phrase, while “good provision” implies the first item’s negative quality.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r11.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r11.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r11.claim: Biqāʿī argues the verse supports the Muʿtazilite view that rizq can include unlawful things.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r6.claim: The verse distinguishes intoxicating drink, which blocks reason and is blameworthy, from wholesome provision such as vinegar and date syrup, which harms neither body nor mind.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r7.speaker: الرماني
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r7.claim: Al-Rummānī transmits from Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Ibrāhīm, al-Shaʿbī, Abū Razīn, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, and Qatāda that intoxicating drink is the prohibited beverage and wholesome provision is lawful drink.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r8.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r8.claim: Some interpreters who take “sukr” to mean intoxicant say its permissibility was abrogated by the prohibition in Sūrat al-Māʾida; the wording already signals disapproval.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r9.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r9.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p284/r9.claim: “Sukr” has four lexical senses: intoxicant, food, stillness, or the verbal noun for intoxication, whose root suggests blockage of channels.

DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r1.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r1.claim: The author's gloss takes good provision as lawful dates and raisins that do not intoxicate.

DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r2.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r2.claim: Ibn Masud says sukar means wine; Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Hasan, al-Shaʿbi, Ibrahim, and Abu Razin report the same.

DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r3.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r3.claim: Qatadah identifies sukar as foreign wines and says the ruling was abrogated in Surat al-Maida.

DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r4.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r4.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr says sukar is forbidden and good provision is lawful.

DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r5.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r5.claim: Hasan says God mentioned wine as a blessing before He prohibited it.

DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r6.speaker: إبراهيم والشعبي
DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r6.claim: Ibrahim and al-Shaʿbi say this ruling is abrogated.

DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r7.speaker: أبو هريرة
DURR-FULL:v5p142#2/r7.claim: A Prophetic report says grapes may be eaten fresh or drunk as juice before drying, then made into raisins or syrup.

DURR-FULL:v5p142/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p142/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p142/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says sukar is forbidden wine, while good provision includes raisins, vinegar, grapes, and their benefits.

DURR-FULL:v5p142/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p142/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p142/r2.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas identifies sukar as nabidh and says the verse was abrogated by the later prohibition in 5:90; Abu Razin says it was revealed before wine was forbidden.

DURR-FULL:v5p142/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p142/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p142/r3.claim: A further gloss makes sukar vinegar and nabidh or similar drinks, and good provision fruit, raisins, and similar foods.

DURR-FULL:v5p142/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p142/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p142/r4.claim: In another report, sugar was later forbidden because it comes from wine, while vinegar, raisins, nabidh, and similar lawful items remain good provision.

DURR-FULL:v5p142/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p142/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p142/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas says people called wine sukar before God later named it khamr when prohibiting it; he says Ethiopians call vinegar sukar.

BURSEVI:v5p38/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p38/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p38/r1.claim: People extract drink and food from dates and grapes; the lexicon defines sukr as wine or date wine.

BURSEVI:v5p38/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p38/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p38/r2.claim: The verse predates wine’s prohibition and signals disapproval by contrasting intoxicant with good provision, since what opposes good is not good.

BURSEVI:v5p38/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p38/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p38/r3.claim: Good provision includes dates, syrup, raisins, date paste, and vinegar; a report calls vinegar the best condiment, and al-Maʾmun recounts using wine vinegar for cough.

BURSEVI:v5p38/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p38/r4.speaker: بعضهم
BURSEVI:v5p38/r4.claim: The wording distinguishes gifts requiring no human processing, for which God says ‘We give you drink,’ from products people must prepare, for which it says ‘you make.’

BURSEVI:v5p38/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p38/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p38/r5.claim: These products are a clear sign for people who use reason to consider the evidence.

BURSEVI:v5p38/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p38/r6.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
BURSEVI:v5p38/r6.claim: Inwardly, dates are fruits of obedience and grapes fruits of spiritual struggle; their yield includes mystical unveilings, visions, and seekers’ extraordinary states.

BURSEVI:v5p38/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p38/r7.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
BURSEVI:v5p38/r7.claim: The ego drinks intoxicating products of spiritual effort and veers from the straight path or displays vanity; heart and spirit receive provision that increases longing, love, sincerity, and seeking.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r1.claim: The opening prepositional phrase attaches to an omitted drink-giving verb, with عصير understood; تتخذون then explains what is taken from the fruit, or the phrase may be parsed in other ways.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhshari offers three syntactic parses and foregrounds the omitted drink-and-juice reading; al-Taybi says his ordering signals preference.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r3.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r3.claim: Abu Hayyan regards the clearest parse as an omitted noun: fruit from the palms and grapes from which you take drink and good provision, with a noun clause coordinated to the earlier one.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r4.claim: The phrase رزقا حسنا can include vinegar, syrup, dates, raisins, and other provisions; some fruits are eaten unripe or left to spoil and feed animals.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r5.speaker: الأخطل
ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r5.claim: Al-Akhtal's line uses سكر as a noun for wine and supports the interpretation of the verse's word as wine.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r6.claim: The word سكر is also explained as a verbal noun, supported by a line that says people came to us drunk and were clear-headed by day.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p179/r7.claim: The verse's partial phrasing suggests that some fruit is consumed before ripeness or is spoiled and eaten by animals.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r1.speaker: الطبري
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r1.claim: Al-Tabari supplies omitted ما after the fruit phrase, meaning some fruit is used to make drink and provision; Abu Hayyan objects that deleting a relative pronoun while retaining its clause is not Basran grammar.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r10.speaker: البيضاوي
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r10.claim: Al-Baydawi hesitates over whether the verse predates the ban: before it, the verse signals dislike; after it, it combines blame and blessing, since wine is paired against good provision.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r11.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r11.claim: Al-Zamakhshari offers either abrogation or a combination of censure and blessing; al-Kashf favors abrogation and reads the juxtaposition as a sign that wine is bad and best avoided.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r12.speaker: ابن كمال
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r12.claim: Ibn Kamal argues that the Meccan verse belongs to a catalogue of great blessings and cannot be reproaching its audience; he therefore places it before the prohibition.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r13.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r13.claim: The milk is attributed to God because humans do not produce it, whereas taking wine is attributed to human action; the final appeal to reason can reinforce a hint against wine.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r2.speaker: ابن كمال
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r2.claim: Ibn Kamal rejects attaching the fruit phrase to an omitted juice-giving verb because that excludes the more important eaten fruit, and challenges the mismatch between juice and the broad provision gloss.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r3.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r3.claim: Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kamal prefer attaching the fruit phrase to تتخذون, reading منه as a repeated prepositional phrase for emphasis; another option attaches it to the sense of feeding in الإسقاء.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r4.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r4.claim: Al-Zamakhshari allows سكر to qualify رزق حسن, so the two would describe a single thing, though al-Alusi notes that coordination normally signals difference.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r5.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عمر وأبو رزين والحسن ومجاهد والشعبي والنخعي وأبو ثور والكلبي وابن جبير
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r5.claim: These authorities and others interpret سكر as wine; the verse was revealed in Mecca, when wine was still lawful, and some say it was abrogated by the later prohibition in 5:90.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas is cited for interpreting سكر as vinegar in the language of Abyssinia; Abu ʿUbayda instead says it is food eaten for pleasure, but al-Zajjaj rejects that account.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r7.speaker: الحنفيون
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r7.claim: The Hanafis reject abrogation and read سكر as non-intoxicating nabidh; they infer permission because God mentions it as a blessing, while intoxication remains forbidden.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r8.speaker: الدارقطني
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r8.claim: A hadith cited from al-Daraqutni says God forbade wine itself, both little and much, and intoxication from every drink.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r9.speaker: إبراهيم النخعي وأبو جعفر الطحاوي وسفيان الثوري
ALUSI-FULL:v14p180/r9.claim: They allow nabidh until it intoxicates; the source notes that al-Thawri himself drank it, citing al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p181/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p181/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p181/r1.claim: The closing phrase describes people who use reason by considering signs; the verb functions intransitively here.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p181/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p181/r2.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v14p181/r2.claim: Abu Hayyan says the closing reference to people of reason matches the opening claim that livestock provide a lesson, since only thoughtful people take lessons.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p181/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p181/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p181/r3.claim: If the passage hints at downgrading wine, the closing appeal to reason presses that point forcefully; wine is called a restraint on intellect, as the cited couplet suggests.

ELMALILI:16:66-67/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:16:66-67/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:16:66-67/r1.claim: This is the first verse revealed about intoxicants; although it does not yet prohibit wine, contrasting intoxicant with good provision shows it is not good.

ELMALILI:16:66-67/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:16:66-67/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:16:66-67/r2.claim: The contrast between intoxicant and good provision parallels the preceding contrast between milk and filth and blood, hinting that intoxicants are impure.

ELMALILI:16:66-67/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:16:66-67/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:16:66-67/r3.claim: Good provision here means molasses and other sweet products.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p202/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p202/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p202/r1.claim: Verse 67 is coordinated with the preceding lesson about livestock.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p202/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p202/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p202/r2.claim: The opening من implies a verb from the previous نسقيكم: God gives drink from the fruits; it does not modify تتخذون, preserving the framing as a divine blessing.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p202/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p202/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p202/r3.claim: This adds one blessing to another; both concern drink and pressing by hand, and Arabs could call pressing grape juice “milking,” as Ḥassān's poem witnesses.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p202/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p202/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p202/r4.claim: The two kinds of drink are related signs; the concluding sign specifically follows the fruit's suitability for pressing and fermentation and its benefits and pleasures, as in Q 16:11.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p202/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p202/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p202/r6.claim: Both instances of من mark source: the first belongs to the implied “We give you drink,” the second to “you make”; the latter is not partitive because intoxicant is not a piece of fruit.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p203/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p203/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p203/r2.claim: Intoxicating drink is mentioned as a pleasure then widespread and permissible; the verse is Meccan, before wine was prohibited in Medina.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p203/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p203/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p203/r3.claim: رزق حسن means beneficial food, especially dates and grapes, sweet and tasty fresh or dried and suitable for storage; grape juice can also become vinegar or syrup.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p203/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p203/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p203/r4.claim: The sign clause is repeated because this is an independent sign; it points to milk, drink, and fruit together, like the sign in Q 16:65.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p203/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p203/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p203/r5.claim: “For people who reason” fits because recognizing the wisdom in milk's formation requires reflection, unlike the obvious sign of rain.

TABATABAI:16:65-67/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:65-67/r6.speaker: المفردات
TABATABAI:16:65-67/r6.claim: Al-Mufradāt distinguishes sukr as a state that clouds reason from sukr as the intoxicating substance that causes that state.

TABATABAI:16:65-77/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:65-77/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
TABATABAI:16:65-77/r1.claim: One no-abrogation interpretation attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās says sukr means vinegar in the Abyssinian language.

TABATABAI:16:65-77/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:65-77/r2.speaker: أبو عبيدة
TABATABAI:16:65-77/r2.claim: Abū ʿUbayda is reported to interpret sukr as a flavorful food or snack, citing a poetic line about making the noble people’s faults one’s food.

TABATABAI:16:65-77/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:65-77/r3.speaker: الحنفيون
TABATABAI:16:65-77/r3.claim: The Hanafis reject abrogation by taking sukr as a non-intoxicating fermented drink; they infer that drinking it below the point of intoxication is permitted because God mentions it among blessings.

TABATABAI:16:65-77/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:65-77/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:16:65-77/r4.claim: The author rejects Ibn ʿAbbās’s foreign-language gloss: where clear Arabic sukr means wine and the proposed Abyssinian meaning means the opposite, using the foreign word would obscure rather than clarify the eloquent text.

TABATABAI:16:65-77/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:65-77/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:16:65-77/r5.claim: He rejects Abū ʿUbayda’s food gloss by referring back to his earlier linguistic argument.

TABATABAI:16:65-77/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:65-77/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:16:65-77/r6.claim: He rejects the Hanafi inference because the verse only says people make such products from fruit; it does not express divine favor toward every lawful or unlawful product, and the contrast with good provision carries reproach.

TABATABAI:16:67-68/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:67-68/r1.speaker: المجمع
TABATABAI:16:67-68/r1.claim: Al-Majmaʿ lists four lexical senses of sukr: intoxicant, a food or taste, stillness, and the verbal noun for bewilderment or clouded perception, illustrating them with poetry and Qurʾānic usage.

TABATABAI:16:67-68/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:67-68/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:16:67-68/r2.claim: The basic sense of sukr is loss of reason through an intoxicating cause; the other meanings derive from it through metaphor or extended usage.

TABATABAI:16:67-68/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:67-68/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:16:67-68/r3.claim: The author cites al-Majmaʿ’s anonymous poems as evidence for sukr meaning taste, stillness, and a wind becoming still; no poets are named.

TABATABAI:16:67-68/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:67-68/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:16:67-68/r4.claim: Grammatically, the phrase from the fruits may be a nominal clause coordinated with the earlier livestock clause, with an omitted what or thing, or a verbal clause coordinated with God sent down, understood as created or granted.

TABATABAI:16:67-68/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:67-68/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:16:67-68/r5.claim: You take from it may stand in apposition or begin an answer to an implied question; the singular pronoun means the mentioned produce, as with the singular pronoun for livestock bellies.

TABATABAI:16:67-68/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:67-68/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:16:67-68/r6.claim: Sukr means intoxicating products such as wine made from dates and grapes, while good provision includes dates, raisins, syrup, and other nourishing foods.

TABATABAI:16:67-68/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:67-68/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:16:67-68/r7.claim: The verse merely enumerates uses of fruit for Meccan polytheists and does not declare alcohol lawful or commend its use; its contrast with good provision may even censure intoxicants, so it states no ruling for later abrogation.

TABATABAI:16:67-68/r8.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:67-68/r8.speaker: صاحب روح المعاني
TABATABAI:16:67-68/r8.claim: Rūḥ al-Maʿānī reports the view that sukr means wine from Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿUmar, Abū Razīn, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, al-Shaʿbī, al-Nakhaʿī, and others.

TABATABAI:16:67-68/r9.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:67-68/r9.speaker: صاحب روح المعاني
TABATABAI:16:67-68/r9.claim: Rūḥ al-Maʿānī argues that the verse is Meccan, wine was then lawful among both righteous and immoral people, and later Medinan prohibition therefore abrogated it.
