TABATABAI:16:67-69/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:67-69/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:16:67-69/r1.claim: Because the verse does not limit the drink by type or amount, treating it as a divine favor would bless all of it without limit and make later condemnation as satanic work a change of mind, which is impossible for God.

TABATABAI:16:67-69/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:67-69/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:16:67-69/r2.claim: The verse’s closing appeal to rational people urges reflection on plants and their fruits.

TABATABAI:16:69-70/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:69-70/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:16:69-70/r4.claim: The signs are matched to different faculties: reviving earth suits listeners as admonition, fruit suits reasoned inference from ordered systems to one manager, and bee life suits reflective thought because its details are subtle.

ASAD-NOTES:16:67#n76/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:16:67#n76/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:16:67#n76/r1.claim: Sakar, intoxicants, contrasts with wholesome sustenance to mark alcohol's positive and negative effects; though revealed earlier than the formal prohibition, the verse already implies moral condemnation.

ASAD-NOTES:16:67#n76/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:16:67#n76/r2.speaker: Ibn 'Abbas
ASAD-NOTES:16:67#n76/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas, as quoted by Tabari, and Razi support the view that the verse already implies alcohol's moral condemnation.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:67/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:67/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:67/r1.claim: Sakar literally means an intoxicating thing; a report attributed to Ibn Abbas takes it specifically as wine.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:67/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:67/r2.speaker: Taberî and some commentators
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:67/r2.claim: Tabari and some commentators read sakar here as drinks not categorically forbidden.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:67/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:67/r3.speaker: most commentators
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:67/r3.claim: Most commentators say sakar’s separation from ‘good provision’ implies it was not commendable, strengthening the sense of an intoxicating drink, although it had not yet been prohibited then.

STUDYQURAN:16:67/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r1.claim: The verse may continue 16:66 by saying God gives drink from cattle and fruits, or say both cattle and fruit exemplify divine instruction.

STUDYQURAN:16:67/r10.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r10.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r10.claim: Sufi writers use wine for maʿrifah, the Divine Presence, and ecstatic spiritual experience; its simultaneous forbidden and sublime meanings drew exoteric criticism, and it became central in poetry by ʿUmar ibn al-Fāriḍ and Rūmī.

STUDYQURAN:16:67/r11.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r11.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r11.claim: Goodly provision means all lawful consumables from the date palm and vine, including fruits and unfermented juices.

STUDYQURAN:16:67/r12.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r12.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r12.claim: Those who understand use reason to contemplate God's signs and proofs and draw lessons from them.

STUDYQURAN:16:67/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r2.claim: The date palm and vine appear elsewhere as blessings and symbolize rich, luxurious gardens.

STUDYQURAN:16:67/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r3.claim: Sakar etymologically means an intoxicating substance, here wine made from grapes or dates.

STUDYQURAN:16:67/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r4.claim: This Makkan verse predates Madinan discouragement and eventual prohibition of intoxicants, which Islamic interpretation understands as a gradual restriction.

STUDYQURAN:16:67/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r5.speaker: Most commentators and legal scholars
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r5.claim: Because Islamic Law forbids intoxicants, most commentators and legal scholars regard this verse as abrogated.

STUDYQURAN:16:67/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r6.speaker: Some
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r6.claim: Some deny technical abrogation: 5:90 explicitly prohibits grape wine, while abrogation requires a clear legal ruling; this verse describes benefits, though it may imply permissibility.

STUDYQURAN:16:67/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r7.speaker: Some commentators
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r7.claim: Some commentators read sakar as nonintoxicating juice, called so because it could ferment and become intoxicating.

STUDYQURAN:16:67/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r8.speaker: Others
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r8.claim: Others identify the drink as nabīdh, date or raisin juice permitted under Ḥanafī law until it becomes intoxicating.

STUDYQURAN:16:67/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r9.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:16:67/r9.claim: Wine remains a spiritual symbol and paradisal pleasure: 47:15 presents it as a Garden river, and 83:25 depicts paradisal wine.
